sn35.92:2.2: The same “duality” is described as the (sentient) body and “external” name and form, which are essential for contact through the six senses ([sn12.19:1.3]()). One person who did deny this duality is Yājñavalkya. This was his culminating philosophy: “For when there is a duality, as it were, then one smells the other, one sees the other, one hears the other, one greets the other, one thinks of the other, one cognizes the other. By what would one cognize that which cognizes this All? By what would one cognize the cognizer?” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). | This raises the question, how are we to reconcile this duality with the “duality” of existence and nonexistence, i.e. eternalism and annihilationsim ([sn22.90:9.2]()).
